entries.title: Trump Offers $5,000 ‘Dividend’ to Every American Adult if Republicans Win Midterms
entries.summary: The president said the payments would come from the economic successes that Democrats will halt if they take back Congress.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump promised to pay every American adult $5,000 if Republicans keep their majorities in Congress in November’s midterms.

“Here is my promise,” Trump said Wednesday, “if the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them — because of our tremendous economic success, like in history, we've never had anything like what's happening, but because of our tremendous strength and success economically — I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”

“That alone should win the midterms,” Trump said, speaking at the party’s midterm convention in Dallas. He added the only condition on the payment, which he dubbed the “Trump dividend,” is that Americans must spend that stimulus in the United States.

There are about 245 million adult citizens in America, meaning Trump’s promise would cost more than $1.2 trillion.

Speaking at the novel Republican midterm convention, Trump compared the proposed payments to a company distributing cash to shareholders and credited his economic policies and tariffs with making them possible.

Federal law bars anyone from offering financial compensation to persuade a voter to cast their ballot in favor of or against a particular candidate.

Trump did not specify when the payments would arrive or detail how the program would be funded. He has previously teased a stimulus payment from tariff money.

Wednesday’s proposal came midway through the president’s remarks in Dallas, where he cast November’s midterms as a choice between preserving his agenda and surrendering gains on immigration, taxes and public safety.

There, he urged Republicans to vote as though he was on the ballot.

“If we lose,” Trump warned, “you're going to lose your border, you're going to lose your tax cuts, you're going to lose your safety and security, you're going to lose your wealth.”

He also pledged to show up for some 35 competitive congressional races before November, promising rallies and town halls to help Republican candidates.

“They might be winning by a little, or losing by a little, or tied,” Trump said. “We can win every one of those races, but I’m going to go to every one of those states for congressmen and for senators.”

That effort, he said, would include returning to Texas to campaign for Ken Paxton for Senate.

Trump touted his economic record, celebrated immigration wins, predicted a swift end to the Iran war and called opposition to transgender women in women’s sports “one of our greatest sound bites of all time.”

More than anything, he said, Trump worried Democrats might switch their positions before Election Day: “I’m petrified that they’ll change.”

“The choice in this election is very, very simple. Democrats are asking you to vote for their failed far-left agendas,” Trump said. “And I'm asking you to let us finish the job we began with the greatest two years in the history of the presidency.”

This story has been updated with further comments from President Trump.
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Fetterman Says He Won’t Leave His Party if Democrats Win the Senate
entries.summary: The Pennsylvania senator’s statement came hours after he made a video cameo at Republicans’ convention.
entries.content:
Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman sought to tamp down speculation about his political future on Wednesday, vowing to remain a Democrat if his party wins the Senate in November.

“I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party-and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on,” Fetterman said in a statement to The Washington Sun.

Fetterman spoke out after his surprise cameo at the Republican convention in Dallas earlier Wednesday night. In a short video appearance, Fetterman criticized democratic socialists and praised his fellow Pennsylvania senator, Republican Dave McCormick. The appearance was highly unusual and drew sharp criticism from some Pennsylvania Democrats.

The senator told The Sun his comments were meant to introduce McCormick “as a great American and friend.”

“We are in different parties, but are both Team PA,” Fetterman said in the statement. “We have delivered hundreds of millions of dollars back to Pennsylvania, fought for improved transportation and affordable housing, and the Steel Way of Life.”

Speculation has grown rampant within both parties about Fetterman’s political future in recent months following his criticism of Democrats while their odds of taking control of the Senate have grown ahead of the November midterms. Some former Fetterman aides have expressed concern he could leave the party in a scenario where Democrats win a Senate majority by a single seat in November, giving him more influence.

Earlier this year, Fetterman said his “red line” for departure would be if the party officially adopts an “anti-Israel” platform. He also set up a joint fundraising committee with McCormick, another highly unusual move that raised eyebrows among his Senate colleagues.

entries.title: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee Loses Democratic Primary
entries.summary: Former CVS executive Helena Foulkes is the first primary challenger to beat a sitting Rhode Island governor in 30 years.
entries.content:
PROVIDENCE, R.I. — Helena Foulkes has defeated Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee in the state’s Democratic primary, ending his bid for a second full term.

McKee’s defeat marks the first time in more than 30 years that a sitting Rhode Island governor has been beaten in a primary. He is the first governor in any U.S. state to lose a party primary since 2018.

Foulkes, a former senior executive at CVS and the retailer Hudson’s Bay, narrowly lost to McKee in a more crowded primary field in 2022, when the governor notably refused to take her concession call.

In their rematch, McKee has been dogged by questions about his administration’s work to replace a critical bridge in the state capital that was abruptly closed due to safety problems in 2023.

Foulkes has leveraged public exasperation over the cost and pace of the bridge project for her argument that McKee's administration isn’t working for most Rhode Islanders.

“People feel like state government just works with a powerful few,” she said. “They don’t think it’s working for them."

McKee, in response, characterized Foulkes as an out-of-touch elite who turned a blind eye to the opioid crisis during her tenure at CVS.

“The option here is somebody who wants to buy this state office who doesn’t have any credibility with their policy thoughts and someone like myself, who has a strong record in terms of working people,” McKee told The Associated Press.

Incumbent governors rarely lose party primaries. The last time it happened in Rhode Island was in 1994, when Democrat Bruce Sundlun lost to state Sen. Myrth York, ending his bid for a third term. In that race, Sundlun was facing multiple controversies and voter fatigue while York ran on reform.

McKee has been governor since 2021, when he stepped into the position after then-Gov. Gina Raimondo was tapped as U.S. commerce secretary.

In 2023, McKee closed the Washington Bridge, a vital link that carries Interstate 195 over the Seekonk River and connects Providence to its eastern suburbs, the south coast of Massachusetts. During the summer, it also carries traffic bound for Cape Cod.

State transportation officials had flagged a “critical failure” in an older part of the bridge, but demolishing and replacing it has taken longer than the governor initially estimated. Traffic continues to flow but has been squeezed into fewer lanes on a newer part of the span. This has led to lengthy commute times for many who cross the bridge daily as signs posted along the bridge thank drivers for their patience.

McKee maintains that his decisions kept people safe and that the bridge construction will be finished by 2028. He often points to Maryland, saying the Washington Bridge will be complete ahead of the replacement of Baltimore's much larger Francis Scott Key Bridge, which collapsed and killed six construction workers in 2024 after a container ship crashed into it.

Foulkes' grandfather and uncle, Thomas and Chris Dodd, were both Democratic U.S. senators in Connecticut. She worked at CVS for 25 years, eventually becoming president of the company’s pharmacy division between 2014 and 2018. She then became chief executive officer of the Canadian retail giant Hudson’s Bay Company before leaving that job in 2020.

When pressed on her time at CVS, Foulkes argued that CVS reduced its opioid dispensing by 40% when she was president of CVS’ pharmacy division. In 2022, after Foulkes had left CVS, the company agreed to pay $5 billion to settle lawsuits nationwide over the toll of opioids without admitting wrongdoing.

The last governor to lose in a primary was former Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer, who narrowly lost the Republican nomination to Kris Kobach in 2018.

In the Republican gubernatorial primary, Aaron Guckian and Elaine Pelino are vying for the nomination. Guckian is a state trade association executive and was the nominee for lieutenant governor in 2022. He won the two-way primary that year with about 68% of the vote. Pelino is a former actor and first-time candidate. The state party has endorsed Guckian.

Notably, Rhode Island’s primary elections are being held on a Wednesday after state lawmakers moved the date from its typical Tuesday election day because it fell too close to Labor Day.

Only four states hold their primary elections in September: Rhode Island, Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Delaware, which has the latest primary date in the U.S., taking place this year on Sept. 15.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Collins Needs to Defy Political Gravity Again — and Trump Isn't Helping
entries.summary: A Canada trade war, an ICE shooting and Iran. How much more can Susan Collins take from Trump and still win?
entries.content:
BATH, Maine — The sun has just emerged from over the Kennebec River, and Republican Sen. Susan Collins is ready to greet workers ahead of the first shift at Bath Iron Works.

Shipbuilders, machinists and welders arrive in fits and starts ahead of the 7 a.m. whistle. Collins and roughly a dozen supporters and campaign staff have one goal: for these union workers to gobble up boxes of T-shirts. The navy blue tees feature “SUSAN” on the pocket (the “USA” in red, white and blue, of course) and “BATH BUILT IS BEST BUILT” displayed around the silhouette of a Navy destroyer.

“T-shirts! Get your T-shirts here!” one staffer yells as workers approach, doing his best impression of a hot dog vendor at a minor league baseball game.

The moment is important for Collins’ team, who confide before the predawn event that it’s a test of sorts. If workers take the shirts? A good sign of where the senator is two months out from Mainers deciding whether to hand her a sixth term in office. And if they don’t? An ominous sign of her prospects.

Luckily for them, medium and 2XL shirts are gone with time to spare before work starts. Even those not taking the shirts are polite enough, telling staffers, “Thanks, I’m all set,” or a straight up “No, thank you,” with minimal hostilities.
Susan_Collins_Bath_09012026_16 copy.jpg (5541x3694, AR: 1.50)There’s a reason the crew was very familiar with Collins. She’s helped steer billions of dollars and years of Pentagon contracts to the shipyard, which is the state’s fourth-largest employer. Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee, has widespread union support, but Collins retains some loyalty among working-class voters.

Collins Argues Her Senate Seniority Translates Into Millions for Maine

It’s part of yet another all-politics-is-local strategy that Collins, the Senate Appropriations Committee chair, is banking on to lock down another term. Check out a sampling of her ads or campaign appearances and the message is clear: She’s responsible for securing money to rebuild a fire station or other local projects that generate jobs. That constituent services work is what Democrats concede is formidable.

“It’s given me a once-in-a-century opportunity to really deliver for the people of Maine. … I have delivered for small communities all across the state,” Collins told The Washington Sun in an interview, noting that 45 new and rebuilt fire stations exist due to federal money she’s brought home. “That matters.”

Despite that pitch, Collins finds herself in yet another reelection dogfight where she’s working to defy political gravity.

She’s the lone Senate Republican representing a state carried by former Vice President Kamala Harris two years ago. But increasingly it’s the impact of President Donald Trump’s policies that is causing her constituents to consider electing a Democrat.

Trump’s Immigration and Trade Policies Cause Headaches 

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and killed a Colombian national in Biddeford, Maine, less than two months ago amid a surge of operations in nearby Portland. But the individual wasn’t the target of the ICE operation, and the fallout has rippled across the state.

More recently, trade negotiations with Canada went belly-up, leading to a nasty break in a longstanding relationship. Collins has pleaded with the administration to resume negotiations, as her state shares a 611-mile border with the neighbor to the north and exported $1.3 billion worth of goods to Canada last year —- 41% of the state’s exports. Instead, the president is posting memes about the Canadian prime minister.

“It is [a lot]. It’s certainly not helpful. There’s no doubt about that,” Collins told The Sun, adding that voters are “perplexed” and “more puzzled than anything” about the Canada trade war.

According to a Fox News poll taken in early August, 59% of voters in the state view Trump unfavorably — and that was before the trade spat.

It’s also not an accident that Collins is trying to put more distance between herself and the president. During an event in Biddeford, Collins called on ICE to enact more reforms beyond the recent equipping of agents with body cameras. She argued the agency should stop making arrests at “sensitive” locales, including schools, hospitals, doctors offices and places of worship.

She also criticized the president’s lack of strategy for launching a war with Iran, which has reached a seventh month and has grown deeply unpopular with Americans.
Pete Hegseth (4987x3325, AR: 1.50)“The president clearly did not have a well-thought-out plan for how to deal with Iran. To me, it was utterly predictable that Iran would close the Strait of Hormuz,” she told reporters. “That should not have come as a surprise, and the administration and the Department of Defense should have been prepared for that.”

Gas prices in the state are averaging more than $4 per gallon. Mainers are also bracing for rising heating oil costs in the coming months, an issue that could crop up closer to Election Day.

The series of events has Collins’ allies wondering how much more of this she can handle and still win. One source close to the longtime senator noted that of all the potential administration-induced impediments that could crop up, a second ICE shooting is the one that worries them the most and could be too difficult to overcome.

“It’s frustrating. It’s almost exhausting,” Jason Levesque, the former Republican mayor of Auburn, Maine, and a political commentator, said of the string of happenings.

Collins has never been a favorite of the president, and the feeling is mutual.

He said in June that she is “not my best friend at all,” all the while touting her vote streak even though “sometimes she voted against me.” While Trump has indicated support for her, there is a gulf between the two, as they don’t have much of a relationship.

“They don’t interact often,” the source close to Collins said, noting that they have cordial interactions when they see each other at White House events.

“She’s not calling him about policy stuff, and he’s not calling her either,” the source added.

Instead, her preferred point of contact in the administration is Vice President JD Vance, who she became friendly with during his brief senatorial tenure.
Vance (2884x1923, AR: 1.50)Vance recently told supporters during a late-August event in the state that Collins has been to the Naval Observatory at least a half-dozen times, yet is “the most independent member” of the Senate and “sometimes makes my job just a little bit harder.”

There’s a different type of independence that will be a factor in November. For the first time during the Trump era, Collins will be running without the president on the ballot.

Although the two are like oil and water politically, they complimented each other well across the state in 2020, with Trump giving Collins a boost in rural areas while she overperformed him along the coast. She toppled Sara Gideon, her Democratic opponent, by 8.5 percentage points and cleared 50%, bypassing the state’s ranked choice system entirely.

This go-round, Collins has sought to beef up her support with some of Trump’s most ardent backers. She repaired what was once a fraught relationship with former Republican Maine Gov. Paul LePage, the favorite to succeed Rep. Jared Golden in the 2nd Congressional District.

She’s relying on her record controlling federal spending bills, including what she has procured for rural areas. Collins has touted that she secured more than $428 million in earmarks for the state. She also has the financial muscle to get that message out after being drowned out by Democratic spending in 2020.

“I know the people of rural Maine. I am one of the people of rural Maine,” she said. “I think people understand authenticity and that they also appreciate how hard I work for rural Maine.”

Collins admits the race against Jackson, the former state Senate president who only entered the race after Graham Platner’s swift exit stage left after being accused of sexual assault, is not the race she expected.

“We had to start all over again,” Collins said. “This is the strangest race I’ve ever seen.”

Democrats Work to Nationalize the Race After Platner’s Messy Exit 

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has maintained a defiant face about the race, repeatedly declaring that this is the year the party topples Collins. Democrats note that Collins’ approval rating has never been lower and that she votes with Trump at a healthy clip. And they stress that Collins’ vote to confirm Trump’s Supreme Court nominees helped put a stake in Roe v. Wade.

But Democrats in the state remain less sure this strategy will work.

One Maine-based Democratic operative argued that the path for Democrats centers around nationalizing the race and keeping Jackson as generic of a candidate as possible, something Republicans are quickly trying to change. Outside groups — and even Collins herself — have pointed to Jackson’s having two children with his longtime partner, who is his second cousin.

“If Democrats and Troy can keep this race about Donald Trump, affordability and what Susan Collins has or hasn’t done to help with those things, put a check on those things, then Troy has a path to victory, even though it is hard,” the operative said.
Troy_Jackson_Lewiston_09012026_26 copy.jpg (5600x3733, AR: 1.50)“The challenge is if this race becomes about Susan Collins versus Troy Jackson or anybody else,” they continued. “Susan Collins versus a specific person is really hard because Susan Collins is not a bad politician.”

Even Jackson’s most ardent supporters acknowledge that overcoming Collins’ long-standing ties is a high hurdle.

“I think he’s got a very challenging road ahead,” Portland’s Democratic mayor, Mark Dion, who was among those introducing Jackson at his first town hall in Lewiston, told The Sun in an interview.

The party is still picking up the pieces after Platner’s implosion in July, which forced party activists to choose a replacement that some voters are still smarting over. During his Lewiston town hall, a self-described independent who votes Democratic pressed Jackson, pointing to advertisements that “keep referring to ‘our movement’ that ‘we built.’”

“It feels disingenuous because the movement that was building was built by someone else,” said Tori Leigh. “You weren’t elected by the voters.”

“You are right. I didn’t build this movement. I’ve been saying that all along,” Jackson responded. “This isn’t about Troy Jackson. But I don’t even think this is about Graham. I think it’s about people across this state that know there’s something fundamentally wrong with the way things are going.”

Jackson peppered the rally with criticisms of Collins, arguing that she has lost touch with the state — citing her decision against holding town hall meetings. The pair recently agreed to four debates, with the first one set for Oct. 6.

The biggest roar at the town hall came when Jackson pressed that ICE should be “eliminated.”

There are also fears of an enthusiasm gap on the left.

Multiple attendees at the Lewiston event were quick to note that Platner held a standing room only event at the same location last fall that also featured a place for an overflow crowd. The Jackson event, meanwhile, featured dozens of empty seats in the back of the room.
Troy_Jackson_Lewiston_09012026_04 copy.jpg (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)The Maine-based Democratic operative argued that while state Democrats have reasons for excitement now, that’s “mostly fueled by being mad at Collins, not excited for Troy.”

Other top Democrats conceded that the winds have shifted since the Platner exodus.

“He’s not a pop star. He’d be the first one to tell you that,” Dion said of Jackson, adding that he is more than willing to trade “pop star status for competency.”

Polling since Jackson’s entrance has been limited, with a pair of surveys taken since the start of August showing him in a lead within the margin of error. Operatives from both parties are quick to note that the state is notoriously hard to poll.

Another question surrounding Jackson is whether he can win over enough independents and Democrats who’ve backed Collins over the years. If the Lewiston event is any indication, he has some work to do.

Tom Soule, a Democrat and a retired school principal from nearby Bowdoinham, noted that he’s supported Collins throughout the years but is considering supporting Jackson in order to more effectively take on Trump. He wasn’t a fan of Platner’s but showed up to check out Jackson’s pitch.

But Jackson’s inability to explain how he would enact change rather than tick through his positions on issues frustrated him.

He ended up leaving the event early, telling The Sun on his way out: “Not impressed.”
entries.author: Al Weaver

entries.title: D.C.’s To-Do List for Janeese Lewis George Keeps Getting Longer
entries.summary: The presumptive mayor-elect has asked D.C. voters to be “brutally honest.” Now comes the hard part.
entries.content:
In the warm, crowded basement of East Washington Heights Baptist Church, Timothy Harrison sat over a plate of soul food, waiting for his opening.

A Ward 7 resident who helps small businesses get off the ground, Harrison didn’t come to point out everything wrong with D.C. He came with a pitch — and a simple philosophy.

“I don’t complain. I want to help her fix this,” Harrison said, gesturing across a room where neighbors were busy scribbling their hopes and frustrations on colored sticky notes. “Anyone can come in with a complaint. But this is the first part of something. That’s why she deserves the right to work.”

Harrison hoped to pitch D.C.’s presumptive next mayor, Council member Janeese Lewis George, on addressing the root trauma of poverty through street-level mental health teams. It was the kind of deep, neighborhood-level dialogue Lewis George built her council career on. She paused by his row to listen, but with hundreds of other residents waiting to get her attention, the physical scale of her new mandate quickly closed in.

“Mayor, we’re running behind,” a staff member interrupted, whisking her away.

By imploring residents to be “unabashedly honest,” Lewis George has opened the floodgates to a city eager to be heard. From working-class residents east of the Anacostia River pleading for basic sanitation to progressive strongholds in Ward 1 demanding she abolish the police department, the first week of her citywide listening tour laid bare the sheer weight of her incoming transition.
_MG_0068 copy.jpg (5909x3940, AR: 1.50)With a clear path to victory awaiting her in November as the Democratic nominee for D.C. mayor, Lewis George has said she is using this in-between period to hunt for low-hanging fruit — policy shifts that don’t require massive budget fights and can also immediately prove to voters that her vision of government works.

But taking in thousands of granular demands also creates the opportunity for immense political friction, as the incoming administration must determine a way to meet voters’ expectations without collapsing beneath them.

It’s a tightrope she acknowledges openly.

“Everything y’all put on this list — the micro and macro things — we’re going to take a check and say, ‘Hey, did you do what you said you were going to do?’” she told the crowd. “We’re basically creating accountability for myself.”

A paper trail of promises

Accountability in government carries a unique and historic burden for residents like Joel Crooms. The 73-year-old says he embodies the wary optimism of a generation that remembers the tangible community investments of past leaders like “mayor for life” Marion Barry — those Crooms felt focused on direct neighborhood needs rather than corporate interests.

He compared Lewis George with the outgoing mayor, Muriel Bowser, whom he accused of prioritizing real estate developers over everyday residents. For Crooms, a resident of Ward 7, Lewis George’s success hinges on breaking that mold.

“As long as she doesn’t sell us out and turn into Bowser in two years,” Crooms said. “But you never know. Money talks.”

At Ward 8’s meeting, 18-year-old Atrayu Lee offered a different kind of generational mandate. A campaign volunteer whose political awakening began by publicly calling out city lawmakers for neglecting youth, the American University freshman challenged the city’s reliance on traditional policing to reduce crime. He implored D.C. leaders to instead make the city’s summer youth-employment program — named after Barry — a year-round affair.

He also urged lawmakers to find a way to get more mental health counselors in D.C. public schools, where he noted supply has failed to meet demand — a hurdle he faced recently as a student at Thurgood Marshall Academy.

“Instead of punishing people for circumstances that may be out of their control, let’s help them and uplift them,” Lee said.
_MG_9892 copy.jpg (5335x3557, AR: 1.50)_MG_9853 copy.jpg (7200x3445, AR: 2.09)Yet the most volatile pressure tests for Lewis George’s progressive platform are surfacing in liberal strongholds like Ward 1, where she captured a commanding 66% of the primary vote. Inside her listening session at All Souls Unitarian Church in Columbia Heights, a friendly reception came paired with sky-high expectations.

Attendees pressed her on a sprawling docket: neighborhood trauma tied to the police department’s past collaborations with ICE; chronic battles over developer-driven displacement; and yawning equity gaps in neighborhood public schools.

The sheer volume of those expectations was visible at every stop on the tour, where residents have been encouraged to write their ideas on sticky notes and place them on oversize poster boards under headers like “Clean Up Trash Here!” and “Other Ideas You Have For Helping Your Community.”

Within hours, bright neon squares would crowd out the printed margin, creating a paper trail of demands calling for everything from 24-hour daycare to traffic-calming speed cameras.

For the thousands of residents who couldn’t cram into the overflowing listening sessions last week, the campaign rolled out an online “people’s survey” to capture even more data, making the solicitation of resident ideas a round-the-clock effort.

Back in Ward 7, Donna Morrow was eager to add to the paper trail. While most attendees staked out a single grievance per sticky note, she filled a bright purple square until her list of neighborhood repairs ran so long it spilled onto a second one.

“I’m gonna start writing them down at home as I think of them,” Morrow said. “Then I’ll call her office.”

From listening to governing 

For Lewis George and her transition team, the citywide tour is designed to function as something of a stress test for her own platform. As her campaign apparatus converts into a governing machine, she’s conceded that the flood of feedback has already forced her to look past her usual legislative playbook.

After hearing an unexpectedly high volume of concerns regarding health care access and provider rollbacks, for example, Lewis George said she directed her team to pivot and more carefully consider how to incorporate the feedback into her administration’s early plans.
_MG_9993 copy.jpg (5219x3479, AR: 1.50)“That’s the difference between legislating and governing,” Lewis George told reporters after the Ward 1 session. “Governing requires me to now take into account some things that maybe I felt personally as a council member. I’m going into these [meetings] open to my mind being changed.”

Lewis George said she’d demonstrate her flexibility well before she’s sworn in. When she returns to the council following summer recess later this month, she intends to put forward legislation aimed at meeting the most urgent constituent demands, setting the stage for immediate executive action when she takes office.

Still, critics and allies alike are watching closely to see if her populist vision can survive the realities of municipal budgeting and other frictions that come with executive power.

The immediate test, Ward 1 Democratic Council nominee Aparna Raj noted, will be how she balances quick administrative wins — like easing small business permits — against the massive, multiyear battles that would likely accompany landmark proposals like social housing or universal child care.

Lewis George insists this pressure is precisely what should drive her administration. Standing among the lingering crowd as another listening session drew to a close, she embraced the challenges ahead.

“I’m less worried about disappointing people and more excited about surprising people,” she said.
entries.author: Michael Brice-Saddler
